question: What does decoding cost before anything is done to make it faster: wall time, processor time and memory, for TrueHD at 2, 6, 8, 12, 14 and 16 channels, for AC-3 and E-AC-3, and for the object formats?
method: `python tools/bench.py --refs --runs 5 --per-kind 2` over the TrueHD heads, the AC-3 and E-AC-3 heads and the clips of the work directory, with a release build of main as it stood after the extractor fix of evidence 04 (rustc 1.99.1) and the machine otherwise idle. The tool runs every command as a process of its own and reads its start and end times, its user and kernel processor time and its peak working set from the operating system; each stream is read once before it is measured; PCM goes to the null device and the object formats to a file. It sorts the streams into kinds by what `info --json` says of them, a TrueHD stream also by the channels of its widest presentation, and measures the two longest and heaviest of each kind. `--refs` times FFmpeg and truehdd on the same streams the same way. The kernels are `cargo bench --locked -p oadec-bench` on the same machine: the decoders called in-process over the committed fixtures, fifteen batches each, the median of the time of one call. `result` is the tool's own record of the run; `python tools/bench.py --report` on this file prints it as a table.

kernels.kernel: eac3: decode the 5.1 core of the object stream
joc: analysis bank, one channel, one frame
joc: synthesis bank, one object, one frame

reading: TrueHD is not where the time is: a 16-channel presentation decodes at 63 to 73 times real time for a little over a second of processor time a minute of audio, memory is flat at 30 MiB whatever the width, and both reference decoders take longer on the same streams (truehdd 1.06 to 3.1 times as long with 2.8 to 6.7 times the processor time; FFmpeg 1.4 to 1.9 times as long on the widest presentation it decodes). The AC-3 family is where it is: the core runs at 83 to 310 times real time and FFmpeg decodes the same frames 4.7 to 6.8 times faster, and `verify` there costs what a decode costs because it decodes. Objects out of JOC cost three to four times the channels under them, 26 to 42 times real time, and the kernels say why: an analysis bank per coded channel and a synthesis bank per object at 37 and 39 microseconds a frame of 32 ms. `verify --decode` is the sum of its presentations. The figures of the decoder alone repeat to within three per cent; the two widest spreads, 35 and 8 per cent, are object files written to a disk. One machine, heads of about a minute, the heaviest streams of each kind and not a sample of what is common: the ratios between commands carry to another machine and the figures do not. An exit code of 7 among the commands is a head that was cut inside a frame; it decodes like any other.
